title: The Manuscript Line: Where the Human Stays

zones.label: Outline From Claims
zones.summary: The first station turns notes into an outline of claims, each tied to its evidence. A person stamps the claim, because the outline fixes the argument.
facts: Outline generation produces the skeleton of the paper with the claim each paragraph will make. It fixes the argument, so your control matters most here (Chapter 15).
Give the agent your notes and results and ask for bullets that are claims naming their evidence. Have it mark any bullet with no evidence supplied. Those marks are the work still to do (Chapter 15).
Each section answers one reader question: the abstract, should I read this; the discussion, what does it mean and what are the limits (Chapter 15).
Write the abstract last, from the finished paper, and make sure every number in it appears in the body (Chapter 15).

zones.label: Drafting From Evidence
zones.summary: The agent drafts only from the supplied claims and evidence, and a number check follows every edit. A person stamps the interpretation.
facts: Draft from claims, not a topic. Supply the claim, the evidence, and the intended reader, and tell the agent to use only that material (Chapter 15).
A marker such as [NO EVIDENCE] keeps a fluent draft from smuggling in claims you cannot support (Chapter 15).
A revision can change numbers and claims without notice while the prose improves. A script that lists numbers found in only the original or only the revision catches it (Chapter 15).
A clean number report does not prove the claims are unchanged, since a qualifier could have been deleted (Chapter 15).
Draft the argument-bearing sections, such as the introduction and discussion, yourself, and give a style sample when you ask for edits (Chapter 15).

zones.label: Figures and LaTeX
zones.summary: Each figure is regenerated by a script from processed data, and the LaTeX is compiled after every substantial edit. The log tells you what the agent broke.
facts: A figure drawn by hand in an editor cannot be reproduced and tends to go stale. Generate every figure from a script that reads the processed data (Chapter 15).
A good caption states what is plotted, the conditions, how to read markers or error bars, and the one observation to take away (Chapter 15).
An agent may use packages the venue's template does not allow or silently alter a macro. Keep the venue's class file unchanged, compile after every substantial edit, and read the log (Chapter 15).
A wrong cross-reference shows up as ?? in the output (Chapter 15).

zones.label: References Checked
zones.summary: References come from verified BibTeX entries and are never retyped. A tag on the belt marks an invented reference that the check caught.
facts: With BibTeX and the venue's style file the formatting is automatic, so the job is keeping each entry correct and complete: venue, year, volume, pages, and DOI (Chapter 15).
Never let an agent retype a reference by hand into the text. That is where fabricated and corrupted entries enter (Chapter 15).
Verify each entry as in Chapter 11 before it goes into the BibTeX file (Chapter 15).
Venue requirements, such as the template, page limit, and required statements, are read before drafting, not after (Chapter 15).

zones.label: Co-Author Consistency
zones.summary: Co-authors read a draft with the claims, evidence, and open questions marked, and the agent proposes consistency fixes as a list. A person stamps the limits.
facts: Technical editing, style consistency, and grammar are agent strengths. Ask for a list of proposed changes and not a silent rewrite, so each can be accepted or rejected in the diff (Chapter 15).
A useful instruction: list inconsistencies in notation and terminology and propose one resolution for each, without editing the text (Chapter 15).
Send co-authors a draft with the claims, evidence, and open questions marked, and ask for specific checks, such as the numbers in Table II (Chapter 15).
Left alone, models drift toward a generic register with claims of significance larger than the evidence (Chapter 15).
Every co-author should know which parts were drafted with AI assistance (Chapter 15).

zones.label: Submit and Respond
zones.summary: A submission box holds the cover letter with a disclosure note attached. The reviewer response claims only changes that were made, and the signature is a person's.
facts: AI systems cannot be authors. Major publishers, including IEEE and ACM, state that they may not be listed and that substantive AI use must be disclosed. Read your venue's current policy (Chapter 15).
A disclosure names the tool, its version or model identifier, the date, and the purpose. A log kept as you work makes the statement accurate (Chapter 18).
A review response quotes each comment, gives your answer, and locates the change. Never claim a change that was not made (Chapter 15).
An agent tends to accommodate every comment. Decide your position first, then ask for wording (Chapter 15).
A cover letter is short and must claim nothing the paper does not (Chapter 15).

quiz.question: A student asks for an outline in which every bullet is a claim that names its evidence, and unsupported bullets are marked. Which region shows this step?
quiz.explanation: The outline fixes the argument, and the marks on unsupported bullets show the work still to be done.

quiz.question: After an agent polishes a paragraph, a script lists a number that appears only in the revision. Which region shows this check?
quiz.explanation: Revision can change numbers without notice while the prose improves, and a before-and-after number comparison catches it.

quiz.question: A figure is regenerated from a script, and a ?? in the compiled output points to a bad cross-reference. Which region shows this?
quiz.explanation: Figures come from scripts that read processed data, and the LaTeX log and output show what an edit broke.

quiz.question: An agent retyped a citation by hand and the paper cites a work that does not exist. Which region shows the control that prevents this?
quiz.explanation: References should come from verified BibTeX entries, because retyping is where fabricated and corrupted entries enter.

quiz.question: A co-author is asked only to check the numbers in one table and to read one section for fairness to prior work. Which region shows this?
quiz.explanation: Co-author review works best with specific requests, a draft that marks the claims and open questions, and a clear note of what AI helped draft.

quiz.question: A reviewer response may list only the changes actually made, and a note about AI use travels with the cover letter. Which region shows this?
quiz.explanation: A claimed change that is missing from the paper destroys trust, and substantive AI use is disclosed instead of listing the tool as an author.

quiz.question: An agent proposes notation and terminology fixes as a list and does not edit the text. Which region shows this working method?
quiz.explanation: A list of proposed changes lets each one be accepted or rejected in the diff, and avoids a silent rewrite.

quiz.question: A prompt supplies only the claim, the evidence, and the intended reader and tells the agent to use nothing else. Which region shows this method?
quiz.explanation: Drafting from supplied claims, with a marker where evidence is missing, stops a fluent draft from adding claims you cannot support.
